According to Mark Gurman's latest issue of the Power On newsletter, Apple is reportedly considering making changes to its App Store. The goal? To boost the potential revenue the platform brings in.

Details of Apple's plans for the App Store remain unclear. Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman reports that Apple wants to "find ways to improve profit margins and squeeze more recurring revenue from the platform," a push being led largely by incoming CEO John Ternus and current Senior Vice President of Services Eddy Cue.

Reportedly, this effort was one of the reasons veteran Apple executive Phil Schiller left the company last week. Schiller stepped down as Senior Vice President of Marketing in 2020 to become an Apple Fellow, with part of his remit including overseeing the App Store. Schiller did not agree with the idea:

Apple has plenty of options to improve the App Store's profit margins. They could get rid of the human app review process — an expensive process that does not achieve much in the age of agentic coding. However, users might not be receptive to further automation of app reviews, even if it helps cut costs.

Apple could raise developer membership fees, currently $99 per year. Given that many small developers are already paying $200 a month for subscriptions to Codex and Claude to build apps, one could argue Apple has room to raise prices and developers would still pay. Apple could also charge large developers subscription fees based on traffic, passing some of the infrastructure costs on to them.

What the end result will be remains to be seen, but I for one am quite curious to see what these changes ultimately look like.
